title: Bidirectional BFS: Split Paths in Salvador
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS fan out from both start and goal, meeting in the middle for fast routes. This visualization turns Salvador’s street layout into a graph search you can actually see.
ig_caption:
🗺️⚡ **Bidirectional BFS in Salvador (Barra)**

Instead of searching from just the start node, **Bidirectional BFS** launches two synchronized BFS frontiers—one from the start and one from the destination—then **terminates when they intersect**. In graph theory terms, we’re searching an **unweighted graph** where intersections reveal the shortest path length with dramatically reduced explored nodes compared to single-source BFS (because the branching factor compounds from only half the distance).

🚦Think of each street intersection as a node and each road segment as an edge on a **real street-map graph**. As the two waves expand, the moment they meet, we reconstruct the route by stitching together the parent pointers from both BFS trees.

🚶‍♂️🧠 **Bidirectional BFS** turns routing into a smart graph search. By running BFS from both the start and the goal at the same time, we cut the search space and quickly find the shortest path on an unweighted street-map graph.

yt_description:
Bidirectional BFS visualization on a real city street graph 🌍⚡
In this YouTube Shorts video, we map Salvador (Barra) intersections as nodes and streets as edges, then run **Bidirectional BFS** from both the start and destination until the frontiers meet. You’ll see how graph search works in an unweighted graph, why it’s faster than standard BFS, and how shortest paths are reconstructed.
